key_terms.meaning: The part of the field of an accelerating charge or a time-varying current that falls as 1/r and carries power away for good.
A = (μ₀/4π) ∫ J e<sup>−jβR</sup>/R dV′: each current element counted as it was R/c seconds earlier; then H = ∇ × A/μ₀.
A uniform current element l ≪ λ: |E<sub>θ</sub>| = 60π I₀ l sin θ/(λr) far away, R<sub>r</sub> = 80π²(l/λ)², D = 1.5.
Power per unit solid angle, U = r²S, in W/sr; P<sub>rad</sub> = ∯ U dΩ.
D = 4πU<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>rad</sub> = 4π/Ω<sub>A</sub>; 1 for an isotropic source; in dBi, 10 log₁₀ D.
G = η<sub>rad</sub> D: directivity reduced by the radiation efficiency; dBd = dBi − 2.15.
Angles between the −3 dB points and between the first nulls of the main lobe; D ≈ 41 253/(θ<sub>E</sub>θ<sub>H</sub>) for one pencil beam, angles in degrees.
P<sub>rad</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub> at a stated point; short dipole with triangular current 20π²(l/λ)², half-wave dipole 73 Ω.
η<sub>rad</sub> = R<sub>r</sub>/(R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>), the share of the accepted power that is radiated.
A<sub>e</sub> = P<sub>r</sub>/S = Gλ²/4π (A<sub>em</sub> = Dλ²/4π lossless); for a dish G = e<sub>ap</sub>(πd/λ)².
PLF = |ρ̂<sub>w</sub> · ρ̂<sub>a</sub>|² = cos²ψ<sub>p</sub> for two linear polarizations; 0.5 (3 dB) for a linear antenna and a circular wave.
r > 2D²/λ with r ≫ D and r ≫ λ (D the largest dimension); reactive near field inside 0.62√(D³/λ).
Cosine current, Z<sub>in</sub> = 73 + j42.5 Ω at exactly λ/2, D = 1.64 (2.15 dBi), HPBW 78°, |E| = 60I₀/r broadside.
Half a dipole on a ground plane: 36.5 + j21.25 Ω, D = 3.28 (5.16 dBi).
Two joined half-wave conductors: R<sub>in</sub> = 4 × 73 = 292 Ω, matches 300 Ω twin-lead.
C ≤ λ/10, a magnetic dipole m = NIA; R<sub>r</sub> = 31 171 (NA/λ²)² = 20π²(C/λ)⁴ for one circular turn.
V<sub>oc</sub> = E l<sub>eff</sub> cos ψ; l<sub>eff</sub> = l (uniform current), l/2 (short dipole), λ/π (half-wave dipole), 2πNμ<sub>eff</sub>A/λ (loop).
Z₁₂ = Z₂₁ for two antennas in a linear medium; pattern, impedance and gain are the same on transmit and receive.
P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub>G<sub>r</sub>(λ/4πd)² = P<sub>t</sub>A<sub>et</sub>A<sub>er</sub>/(λ²d²) in the far field and free space.
FSPL(dB) = 32.44 + 20 log₁₀ f<sub>MHz</sub> + 20 log₁₀ d<sub>km</sub>; P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> + G<sub>t</sub> + G<sub>r</sub> − FSPL − losses; margin = P<sub>r</sub> − P<sub>sens</sub>.

takeaways: Only accelerating charge, that is a time-varying current, radiates; the radiated field falls as 1/r, and its power density as 1/r².
The Hertzian dipole’s fields come from the retarded vector potential and have 1/r, 1/r² and 1/r³ terms that are equal at r = λ/2π; far away only the 1/r term with its sin θ pattern is left.
Directivity, gain and beamwidth reduce a pattern to numbers: D = 4π/Ω<sub>A</sub>, G = η<sub>rad</sub>D, and the HPBW sits at the −3 dB (field 0.707) points.
Radiation resistance must be quoted with its current convention: 80π²(l/λ)² for uniform current, 20π²(l/λ)² for a real short dipole, 73 Ω for a half-wave dipole.
Small antennas have tiny R<sub>r</sub>, so loss resistance takes most of the power; a λ/20 dipole with 0.5 Ω of loss radiates only half its input.
Every antenna has A<sub>em</sub> = Dλ²/4π, so a thin wire can capture power from an area much larger than its metal.
Far-field formulas need r > 2D²/λ for large antennas and a few wavelengths for small ones; a 0.6 m dish at 12 GHz needs 28.8 m.
The half-wave dipole (73 Ω, 2.15 dBi), the monopole (36.5 Ω, 5.16 dBi) and the folded dipole (292 Ω) are the workhorse wire antennas; a small loop is a magnetic dipole with R<sub>r</sub> ∝ (size)⁴.
Reciprocity (Z₁₂ = Z₂₁) lets an antenna measured on transmit be used on receive with the same pattern, impedance and gain.
In decibels the Friis equation is a sum; the link margin P<sub>r</sub> − P<sub>sens</sub> must stay positive with room for fading.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the Hertzian dipole fields from the vector potential, the definitions of the antenna parameters with a numerical problem, and a Friis link-budget or far-field calculation; the half-wave dipole, the monopole and the small loop are the usual antennas for “derive and compare” questions.

bank.q: Explain the radiation mechanism of an antenna. Why does a charge moving at constant velocity not radiate while an accelerating charge does? How does a two-wire line become a radiator?
outline: Static charge and steady current: fields tied to the source, nothing leaves
Constant velocity: field lines move with the charge, no kink
Acceleration: a kink forms and travels outward at c as the radiation field
l dI/dt = q dv/dt: a time-varying current is accelerating charge
Two-wire line: opposite currents cancel; flared into a dipole they add and radiate
Radiated field falls as 1/r and power density as 1/r²
answer: Radiation is a field that leaves its source and keeps travelling, carrying power to any distance. Its electric field falls as 1/r, so its power density falls as 1/r², and the power crossing any sphere round the source is the same: it never returns.

A charge at rest has radial field lines fixed to it; a steady current has a magnetic field fixed to the wire. Neither changes with time, so nothing travels away. A charge moving at constant velocity drags its field pattern with it unchanged; at every point the field simply follows the charge, again with no outward wave.

Now let the charge accelerate for a short time. Information about the change spreads at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Beyond a radius ct the field lines still point to where the charge would have been; inside it they point to its new position. Between the two a kink forms. The kink is a transverse field that moves outward at c and is no longer attached to the charge: that is radiation. The faster the acceleration, the sharper the kink and the stronger the radiated field.

In a wire of length l carrying charge q, a change of current is a change of velocity of the charge: l dI/dt = q dv/dt. So a time-varying current radiates, and a sinusoidal current, which accelerates its charges all the time, radiates all the time. A DC current does not radiate; switching it off suddenly radiates a short pulse.

A two-wire transmission line carries equal and opposite currents on two wires a small distance apart. Their fields cancel almost completely at a distance, so the line guides power without radiating. Bend the last λ/4 of each wire outward until the two are in line. The currents on the two arms now flow in the same direction, so their fields add instead of cancelling, and the open end of the line has become a half-wave dipole that radiates strongly. An antenna is therefore a transition between a guided wave and a free-space wave.

answer.text: The field of a small current element shows both parts of the field at once:
answer.pre:
E<sub>θ</sub> ∝ [1/r (radiation) + 1/r² (induction) + 1/r³ (electrostatic)]
terms equal at r = λ/2π; only the 1/r term reaches far away

answer: The usual picture of a dipole shows it clearly. In the first quarter cycle charges separate to the two arms and field lines stretch from one arm to the other. In the next quarter cycle the charges return and the ends of each field line move back towards the feed; the outer part of the line cannot follow at once, so the line closes on itself into a loop and breaks away. A new set of loops with the opposite direction forms in the next half cycle and pushes the first outward. The detached loops, spaced λ/2, travel outward at c: the radiated wave.

Radiation therefore needs (a) a time-varying current, (b) a structure whose currents do not cancel at a distance, and (c) a size that is not negligible against λ, since the radiated power grows as (l/λ)² for a short element.

Check with numbers: a Hertzian element 1 cm long carrying 1 A at 1 GHz (l/λ = 0.0333) radiates P<sub>rad</sub> = 40π²(I₀ l/λ)² = 0.439 W, while the same 1 A as a steady current radiates nothing. At 100 m its field is 62.8 mV/m and at 1 km 6.28 mV/m, a tenth: the 1/r law of radiation.

bank.q: Define radiation pattern, radiation intensity, beam solid angle, directivity, gain and half-power beamwidth. How is gain related to directivity? Find D, G and HPBW for a field pattern sin θ with 90 % efficiency.
outline: Pattern: field or power against angle; E-plane and H-plane cuts; lobes and nulls
U = r²S in W/sr; Ω<sub>A</sub> = ∯ P<sub>n</sub> dΩ
HPBW between −3 dB points; FNBW between first nulls
sin θ pattern: HPBW 90°, D 1.5, G 1.35
answer: Radiation pattern: the far-field strength plotted against direction (θ, φ) at a fixed large distance, normalised to its peak. A field pattern plots |E|, a power pattern |E|², a dB pattern 10 log₁₀ of the power pattern. Two cuts are drawn: the E-plane (containing E and the peak direction) and the H-plane (containing H). The pattern has a main lobe, minor lobes (side and back lobes) and nulls.

Radiation intensity U = r²S, the power per unit solid angle in W/sr. Since S falls as 1/r² in the far field, U depends only on direction. The total power is P<sub>rad</sub> = ∯ U dΩ, with dΩ = sin θ dθ dφ.

Beam solid angle Ω<sub>A</sub> = ∯ P<sub>n</sub> dΩ, with P<sub>n</sub> = U/U<sub>max</sub>: the solid angle through which all the power would flow if the intensity were U<sub>max</sub> inside it and zero outside.
Directivity D = 4πU<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>rad</sub> = 4π/Ω<sub>A</sub>: the peak intensity over the average intensity. An isotropic source has D = 1 (0 dBi).

Gain G = η<sub>rad</sub>D, where η<sub>rad</sub> = P<sub>rad</sub>/P<sub>in</sub> is the radiation efficiency. Losses lower the radiated power but not the pattern shape, so G ≤ D and G = D only for a lossless antenna. Both are quoted in dBi.

Half-power beamwidth: the angle between the two directions of the main lobe where the power is half the peak (−3 dB), that is the field is 0.707 of the peak. First-null beamwidth: the angle between the first nulls either side; it is wider.

answer.text: Worked case, F(θ) = sin θ, no φ dependence:

answer: First-null beamwidth for the same pattern: the field sin θ is zero only at θ = 0° and 180°, so FNBW = 180°; the main lobe fills the whole half-plane between the nulls. Side-lobe level and front-to-back ratio have no meaning here, because the dipole has two equal lobes and no minor lobes.

answer.text: A contrasting pattern shows why beamwidth alone is not enough. Take U = U₀ cos²θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 90° only:
answer.pre:
P<sub>rad</sub> = 2πU₀/3,  D = 4πU₀/(2πU₀/3) = 6.00 (7.78 dBi)
HPBW = 90° in every plane (cos²θ = 0.5 at θ = 45°)
estimate 41 253/(90 × 90) = 5.09 (7.07 dBi), 0.71 dB low

answer: Both patterns have a 90° HPBW in the plane through the axis, yet their directivities differ by a factor of four, because the second also has a 90° beam in the other plane and sends nothing into the lower half.

Check: the estimate 41 253/(θ<sub>E</sub>θ<sub>H</sub>) cannot be used here, since the H-plane pattern of this antenna is omnidirectional (no beamwidth). The exact value D = 1.5 is also the Hertzian dipole’s, consistent with P<sub>rad</sub> and S in that chapter: S = 1.5 × 0.439/(4π × 100²) = 5.24 µW/m², equal to |E|²/2η with |E| = 62.8 mV/m.

bank.q: Distinguish radiation resistance, loss resistance and input impedance of an antenna, and define radiation efficiency. A centre-fed dipole λ/20 long has 0.5 Ω of loss; find its R<sub>r</sub>, efficiency and gain.
outline: R<sub>r</sub>: P<sub>rad</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub> at a stated point; current conventions
R<sub>L</sub>: conductor, dielectric and coil loss
Z<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> + jX<sub>A</sub>; resonance means X<sub>A</sub> = 0, not high efficiency
answer: Radiation resistance R<sub>r</sub>: the fictitious resistance that would absorb the radiated power when the antenna current flows through it, P<sub>rad</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub> with I the peak current at a stated point (feed or current maximum). It is not a physical resistor and cannot be measured with an ohmmeter; it exists only at the working frequency.

The value depends on the current convention. Uniform current (Hertzian dipole): R<sub>r</sub> = 80π²(l/λ)². A real centre-fed short dipole has current falling linearly to zero at the tips, half the average current and so a quarter of the power for the same feed current: R<sub>r</sub> = 20π²(l/λ)². Half-wave dipole: 73 Ω; quarter-wave monopole: 36.5 Ω.

Loss resistance R<sub>L</sub>: the series resistance that accounts for power turned into heat in the conductors (raised by the skin effect, rising as √f), in the dielectric and in any loading coil or matching network.

Input impedance Z<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> + jX<sub>A</sub>: what the feed line sees at the terminals. The reactance X<sub>A</sub> comes from energy stored in the near field. At resonance X<sub>A</sub> = 0; resonance makes matching easy but says nothing about efficiency.

Radiation efficiency: the same current flows through R<sub>r</sub> and R<sub>L</sub>, so η<sub>rad</sub> = P<sub>rad</sub>/P<sub>in</sub> = R<sub>r</sub>/(R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>), and the gain is G = η<sub>rad</sub>D.

answer.text: Numerical case, l = λ/20, R<sub>L</sub> = 0.5 Ω, D = 1.5:

answer: Interpretation: half the input power heats the antenna, and the loss more than cancels the 1.76 dBi of directivity. Shortening to λ/50 (R<sub>r</sub> = 0.079 Ω) drops η<sub>rad</sub> to 0.14; lengthening to λ/10 (1.97 Ω) raises it to 0.80. A half-wave dipole, at 73 Ω, is above 99 % efficient with the same 0.5 Ω (73/73.5 = 0.993).

How a designer raises the efficiency of a short antenna: (1) raise R<sub>r</sub>, by top loading (a capacitance hat makes the current nearly uniform, moving R<sub>r</sub> from the 20π² towards the 80π² value, up to four times) or by making the antenna longer; (2) lower R<sub>L</sub>, with thicker or silver-plated conductors and a high-Q loading coil; (3) keep lossy materials away from the strongest fields.

Matching is a separate problem: the input of a short dipole is a fraction of an ohm in series with a large capacitive reactance, so a matching network is needed. Its own loss adds to R<sub>L</sub>, which is why a well-matched short antenna can still be inefficient.

Separating R<sub>r</sub> from R<sub>L</sub> in practice: a network analyser measures only R<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>. The Wheeler cap method measures the input resistance twice, once in free space and once inside a closed metal cap that stops radiation without touching the near field; inside the cap only R<sub>L</sub> remains, so η<sub>rad</sub> = (R<sub>free</sub> − R<sub>cap</sub>)/R<sub>free</sub>.
Check: P<sub>in</sub> split for 1 A peak: ½ × 1² × 0.493 = 0.247 W radiated and ½ × 1² × 0.5 = 0.25 W lost, a ratio of 0.497 as found.

bank.q: Write the Friis transmission equation, derive it, explain every symbol and state the assumptions under which it is valid.
outline: Assumptions: far field, free space, aligned, polarization and impedance matched
answer: Let a transmitter radiate P<sub>t</sub> watts. An isotropic antenna spreads it evenly over a sphere of area 4πd², so the power density at distance d is P<sub>t</sub>/(4πd²) W/m².
A transmitting antenna of gain G<sub>t</sub>, pointed at the receiver, multiplies this by G<sub>t</sub>: S = P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub>/(4πd²). The product P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub> is the EIRP.
The receiving antenna delivers S times its effective aperture A<sub>er</sub> = G<sub>r</sub>λ²/4π to a matched load:

answer.text: Result:
answer.pre:
P<sub>r</sub> = [P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub>/(4πd²)] × [G<sub>r</sub>λ²/4π]
    = P<sub>t</sub> G<sub>t</sub> G<sub>r</sub> (λ/4πd)²

answer: Symbols: P<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>t</sub> received and transmitted power in W; G<sub>t</sub>, G<sub>r</sub> antenna gains as plain ratios; λ the wavelength and d the separation, in the same unit (metres). (4πd/λ)² is the free-space path loss, the spreading of the wave, not absorption.
In decibels: P<sub>r</sub>(dBm) = P<sub>t</sub>(dBm) + G<sub>t</sub>(dBi) + G<sub>r</sub>(dBi) − FSPL(dB), with FSPL = 32.44 + 20 log₁₀ f<sub>MHz</sub> + 20 log₁₀ d<sub>km</sub>.

Assumptions: (1) far field at both ends, d > 2D²/λ and d ≫ λ; (2) free space, with a clear line of sight and no ground reflection, multipath, rain or gas absorption; (3) antennas pointed at each other (gains are taken in the direction of the other antenna); (4) polarizations matched, otherwise multiply by the PLF; (5) impedances matched, otherwise multiply by 1 − |Γ|² at each end; (6) losses in feeders added separately.

Aperture form: putting both gains as apertures, G = 4πA<sub>e</sub>/λ², gives P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>A<sub>et</sub>A<sub>er</sub>/(λ²d²). With fixed gains the received power falls as f²; with fixed antenna sizes it rises as f², because each aperture’s gain grows faster than the spreading loss.

EIRP = P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub> collects the transmitter side into one number; the receiving side is G<sub>r</sub>, and the path is FSPL. Each doubling of distance or of frequency (fixed gains) adds 6.02 dB to the FSPL.

A dB-form example of the same link with a 2 dB cable loss and 6 dBi antennas: P<sub>r</sub> = 20 + 6 + 6 − 80.05 − 2 = −50.05 dBm. Each dB of antenna gain or cable loss enters once, at its own end of the link.

Why the gains are taken in the direction of the other antenna: G(θ, φ) is a function of direction, and only the value along the line joining the two antennas matters. A dish whose half-power beamwidth is 1.5°, pointed 0.75° off, loses 3 dB at that end, which Friis counts as a lower G<sub>t</sub> or G<sub>r</sub>.

Check with numbers: 100 mW at 2.4 GHz (λ = 0.125 m) between 0 dBi antennas 100 m apart: (λ/4πd)² = (0.125/1256.6)² = 9.89 × 10⁻⁹, so P<sub>r</sub> = 0.1 × 9.89 × 10⁻⁹ = 9.89 × 10⁻¹⁰ W = −60.05 dBm; in dB, 20 dBm − 80.05 dB = −60.05 dBm. The two forms agree.

bank.q: An infinitesimal dipole of length λ/50 carries a uniform current of 2 A peak at 300 MHz. Find its radiation resistance, the power radiated and the far field at 1 km broadside. If its loss resistance is 1 Ω, find its efficiency.
answer: Wavelength: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(300 × 10⁶) = 1 m, so l = λ/50 = 0.02 m = 2 cm and l/λ = 0.02. The current is uniform, so the Hertzian formulas apply.

answer.text: Radiation resistance and power:

answer: Far field at r = 1 km broadside (θ = 90°): βr = 2π × 1000 = 6283 ≫ 1, so only the 1/r term is needed. |E<sub>θ</sub>| = ηβI₀l sin θ/(4πr) = 60πI₀l/(λr) = 60π × 2 × 0.02/(1 × 1000) = 7.54 × 10⁻³ V/m = 7.54 mV/m.
Magnetic field: |H<sub>φ</sub>| = |E<sub>θ</sub>|/η = 7.54 × 10⁻³/377 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ A/m.
Cross-check through directivity (D = 1.5): S = DP<sub>rad</sub>/(4πr²) = 1.5 × 0.632/(4π × 10⁶) = 7.54 × 10⁻⁸ W/m², and √(2ηS) = √(2 × 377 × 7.54 × 10⁻⁸) = 7.54 × 10⁻³ V/m. The two routes agree.

answer.text: Efficiency with R<sub>L</sub> = 1 Ω:

answer: Comment: a λ/50 element is a poor radiator. Its R<sub>r</sub> is a fraction of an ohm, so ordinary losses take three quarters of the input, and the tiny resistance with a large capacitive reactance makes it hard to match. If the current tapered to zero at the tips (a real short dipole), R<sub>r</sub> would be a quarter of this, 0.079 Ω, and the efficiency would fall to 0.073.
Field off broadside: the pattern is sin θ, so at θ = 30° the field at 1 km is 7.54 × 0.5 = 3.77 mV/m and along the wire it is zero.

Near-field check: at r = 10 cm, βr = 0.628, so the 1/(βr) and 1/(βr)² terms (1.59 and 2.53) are larger than the radiation term; the far-field formula would be badly wrong there. Far-field formulas are safe from about 1.6λ = 1.6 m.

answer.text: Comparison with a half-wave dipole carrying the same 2 A:

answer: Why the formula for uniform current is the right one here: the question says “infinitesimal dipole” and “uniform current”, which is the Hertzian model (l<sub>eff</sub> = l). A practical short wire without top loading would have a triangular current and a quarter of this R<sub>r</sub>; an examiner expects the convention to be stated.
Power density at 1 km from the element: 7.54 × 10⁻⁸ W/m², which is 1.5 times the 5.03 × 10⁻⁸ W/m² an isotropic source of 0.632 W would give: the 1.76 dB of directivity of every short dipole.
Check: P<sub>rad</sub> ∝ (l/λ)², so a λ/10 element with the same current would radiate 25 times more, 15.8 W, with R<sub>r</sub> = 7.9 Ω.

bank.q: A half-wave dipole radiates 10 W. Find the radiation intensity, the power density and the electric field strength at 5 km in the broadside direction. Check the field from the feed current.
answer: Data: P<sub>rad</sub> = 10 W, half-wave dipole D = 1.64 (2.15 dBi), r = 5 km = 5000 m, broadside θ = 90°, which is the direction of maximum radiation. At 5 km the dipole is far in its far field for any usual frequency.
Maximum radiation intensity: U<sub>max</sub> = DP<sub>rad</sub>/4π = 1.64 × 10/12.566 = 1.305 W/sr.
Power density: S = U<sub>max</sub>/r² = 1.305/(5000)² = 5.22 × 10⁻⁸ W/m² = 52.2 nW/m².

answer.text: Check from the feed current:

answer: The two values, 6.27 and 6.28 mV/m, agree; the small gap is the rounding of 73 Ω (73.1) and 1.64 (1.641).

answer.text: Summary:

answer: Comparison with an isotropic source of the same 10 W: S<sub>iso</sub> = 10/(4π × 25 × 10⁶) = 3.18 × 10⁻⁸ W/m². The dipole’s broadside density is 1.64 times this, the 2.15 dB of directivity.
Off broadside the field follows F(θ) = cos((π/2) cos θ)/sin θ. At θ = 60° (30° above the broadside direction) F = cos(45°)/sin 60° = 0.7071/0.8660 = 0.816, so |E| = 0.816 × 6.27 = 5.12 mV/m.

Received power, if the frequency is 100 MHz (λ = 3 m) and the receiver is another matched half-wave dipole broadside on: A<sub>em</sub> = 1.64 × 9/4π = 1.175 m², so P<sub>r</sub> = S A<sub>em</sub> = 5.22 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.175 = 6.13 × 10⁻⁸ W = −42.1 dBm.

Why broadside: the half-wave dipole’s pattern is a doughnut with its maximum at θ = 90° in every direction round the wire, so the value of D = 1.64 applies there and only there. Along the wire (θ = 0°) the field is zero.

Units and the meaning of each quantity: U (W/sr) does not depend on distance; S (W/m²) falls as 1/r²; |E| (V/m) falls as 1/r. Halving the radiated power to 5 W would lower U and S by half and |E| by √2, to 4.43 mV/m.

answer.text: A self-consistency check that links D, R<sub>r</sub> and the field formula:
answer.pre:
U<sub>max</sub> = r²|E|²/(2η) = (60 I₀)²/(240π) = 15 I₀²/π
P<sub>rad</sub> = ½ I₀² × 73 = 36.5 I₀²
D = 4π U<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>rad</sub> = 60/36.5 = 1.644

answer: So the three textbook numbers for the half-wave dipole, |E| = 60I₀/r, R<sub>r</sub> = 73 Ω and D = 1.64, are one result seen three ways; any two give the third.
Check of the 1/r law: at 10 km the field would be half, 3.14 mV/m, and the power density a quarter, 1.31 × 10⁻⁸ W/m².

bank.q: A 900 MHz link spans 12 km. The transmitter gives 2 W and both antennas are half-wave dipoles (2.15 dBi). Compute the received power in dBm by a link budget and check it with the ratio form of Friis. Is there margin for a receiver of sensitivity −100 dBm?
answer: Data: P<sub>t</sub> = 2 W, f = 900 MHz, d = 12 km, G<sub>t</sub> = G<sub>r</sub> = 2.15 dBi (ratio 1.64), no feeder loss given, receiver sensitivity −100 dBm.
Wavelength: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(9 × 10⁸) = 0.333 m. Far field: the dipoles are 0.17 m long, so 12 km is far beyond any near field.
Transmit power in dBm: 10 log₁₀(2000 mW/1 mW) = 33.01 dBm.
Free-space path loss: FSPL = 32.44 + 20 log₁₀ 900 + 20 log₁₀ 12 = 32.44 + 59.08 + 21.58 = 113.11 dB. Check with 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) = 20 log₁₀(4π × 12 000/0.333) = 20 log₁₀(452 389) = 113.11 dB.

answer.text: Link budget:
Ratio form of Friis:

answer: Both forms give −75.8 dBm (26.3 pW). The margin, P<sub>r</sub> − P<sub>sens</sub> = −75.8 − (−100) = 24.2 dB, is a healthy fade margin for a fixed link.

Caveats: Friis assumes free space. A real 12 km path at 900 MHz near the ground has reflection and obstruction losses, typically far more than free space, so the 24 dB margin would be used up quickly by a ground-level path; masts high enough to clear the first Fresnel zone are needed (see ground, sky and space wave propagation). Feeder loss, if present, comes straight off the margin.

answer.text: A third route, through the field at the receiver:

answer: Free-space range limit: the 24.2 dB margin would allow the distance to grow by 10<sup>24.2/20</sup> = 16.2 times, to about 195 km, before P<sub>r</sub> reached −100 dBm. No real ground-level 900 MHz path reaches that, which shows how much of a real budget goes to the terrain and not to free-space spreading.
Gain in the ratio form must be 1.64, not 2.15: putting dB values into the product is the commonest slip in this question. Likewise d and λ must be in the same unit (12 000 m and 0.333 m).
Received voltage: 26.3 pW in a matched 50 Ω receiver input corresponds to a peak voltage √(2PR) = √(2 × 2.63 × 10⁻¹¹ × 50) = 51 µV (36 µV rms), comfortably above typical receiver noise.
Effect of feeders: if each end had 2 dB of cable loss, P<sub>r</sub> would drop to −79.8 dBm and the margin to 20.2 dB. Every decibel of loss anywhere in the chain comes straight off the margin.

Clearance check for the free-space assumption: the radius of the first Fresnel zone at mid-path is √(λd₁d₂/d) = √(0.333 × 6000 × 6000/12 000) = 31.6 m, so the line of sight must clear the ground and obstacles by tens of metres for Friis to hold.
Check of sensitivity to distance: doubling to 24 km adds 6.02 dB of FSPL, giving −81.8 dBm and an 18.2 dB margin.

bank.q: Find the reactive near-field limit and the far-field distance of a 1.2 m dish at 6 GHz, and state which region a 20 m measurement distance lies in. What happens to a pattern measured there?
outline: 20 m is in the radiating near field (Fresnel)
Measured beam broadened, nulls filled, side lobes wrong
answer: Wavelength: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(6 × 10⁹) = 0.05 m. The dish is D = 1.2 m = 24λ across, an electrically large antenna, so the aperture rules apply.

answer.text: Boundaries:

answer: The far-field rule also needs r ≫ D and r ≫ λ: 57.6 m is 48 dish diameters and 1152 wavelengths, so both hold.

answer.text: Regions:

answer: 20 m lies between 3.64 m and 57.6 m: the radiating near field. The stored reactive fields are negligible there, but the path difference from the centre and the rim of the dish to the probe is D²/(8r) = 1.44/160 = 9.0 mm = 0.18λ, a phase error of 65°, far above the π/8 (22.5°) allowed.

Effect on the measurement: the rays from different parts of the dish do not arrive in the phase they would at infinity, so the measured main beam is broader, its peak lower, the first nulls are filled in and the side lobes merge into a shoulder. The gain read from such a measurement is too low. To measure correctly, use at least 57.6 m, or a compact range, or a near-field scanner with a far-field transformation.
Which frequency would make the 20 m range enough for this dish? Require 2D²/λ ≤ 20 m: λ ≥ 2 × 1.44/20 = 0.144 m, that is f ≤ 2.08 GHz. At 6 GHz the range must be almost three times longer.

In the reactive region (inside 3.64 m) the probe would also couple to the stored fields of the feed and the rim, loading the antenna and changing its input impedance; no pattern measurement is meaningful there.

How far the reactive and radiating regions reach in wavelengths: 3.64 m is 73λ and 57.6 m is 1152λ. For an electrically large antenna both distances are many wavelengths, so the wavelength rule (1.6λ = 0.08 m) never decides.

Practical note: outdoor ranges for such dishes are often built between two towers or rooftops to keep ground reflections out, which is another reason to keep the range as short as the far-field rule allows.
Check: at 57.6 m, D²/(8r) = 1.44/460.8 = 3.125 mm = λ/16, exactly the π/8 phase error that defines the boundary.

bank.q: A folded dipole is fed by a 300 Ω twin line. Show numerically why the folded dipole suits this feed better than a plain half-wave dipole: compare reflection coefficient, VSWR, return loss and mismatch loss.
outline: Folded dipole: equal currents in both conductors, R<sub>in</sub> = 4 × 73 = 292 Ω
Return loss −20 log|Γ|; mismatch loss −10 log(1 − |Γ|²)
Folded: VSWR 1.03; plain: VSWR 4.11, 2 dB lost
answer: Plain half-wave dipole, cut to resonance: R<sub>in</sub> ≈ 73 Ω. Folded dipole: two parallel half-wave conductors joined at the ends; in the antenna mode both carry the same current I in the same direction. For a feed current I the radiating current is 2I, so the field is doubled and, for the same feed current, the power is four times larger: R<sub>in</sub> = 2² × 73 = 292 Ω.
On a line of characteristic impedance Z₀ = 300 Ω, Γ = (Z<sub>L</sub> − Z₀)/(Z<sub>L</sub> + Z₀), VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), return loss RL = −20 log₁₀|Γ| and mismatch loss ML = −10 log₁₀(1 − |Γ|²).

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: The folded dipole is almost a perfect match: less than 0.02 % of the power is reflected. The plain dipole reflects 37 % of the incident power and loses 2 dB, and the standing wave (VSWR 4.1) raises the peak voltage on the line and makes the input impedance at the receiver depend on the line length.

A second benefit: the folded dipole’s two conductors act like one fat conductor, so its reactance changes more slowly with frequency and its bandwidth is wider than a thin dipole’s. Its pattern, directivity (1.64) and gain are the same as the plain dipole’s, because the current distribution is the same.
If 75 Ω coax must feed the folded dipole, a λ/2 coaxial balun gives a 4 : 1 step (75 × 4 = 300 Ω) and also converts unbalanced to balanced.

Feeding from 75 Ω coaxial cable instead: a folded dipole connected directly gives Γ = (292 − 75)/(292 + 75) = 0.591 and VSWR 3.89, a 1.87 dB mismatch loss, and the unbalanced coax would also carry current on its shield. Through a 4 : 1 balun the folded dipole looks like 292/4 = 73 Ω on the coax side, Γ = −0.0135 again.

A large VSWR also raises the voltage maxima on the line by the factor 1 + |Γ| (1.61 for the plain dipole on 300 Ω), which matters for transmitters, and makes the impedance seen by the radio swing with line length.

Why the folded dipole steps up by exactly 4: the two conductors are so close (s ≪ λ) that each carries the same current in the antenna mode; the radiated field depends on the total current 2I, while the feed sees only I. With conductors of different diameters the step-up ratio departs from 4, which designers use to hit other impedances.
Power accounting with 100 W incident on the line: the folded dipole reflects 0.018 W and accepts 99.98 W; the plain dipole reflects 37 W and accepts 63 W, the 2.01 dB mismatch loss of the table.
Check: with three equal conductors the step-up is 3² = 9, giving 657 Ω, which would suit neither line: two conductors is the right choice for 300 Ω.

bank.q: Compare the half-wave dipole, the quarter-wave monopole and a small loop as the antenna of a 433 MHz low-power sensor. Discuss size, impedance, efficiency and pattern, with numbers, and recommend one.
outline: Dipole: 0.33 to 0.35 m, 73 Ω, 2.15 dBi, balanced, needs a balun
Monopole: 0.173 m, 36.5 Ω, needs a ground plane, 5.16 dBi ideal
Small loop: C ≤ 6.9 cm, R<sub>r</sub> ≈ 0.02 Ω, η about 16 % with 0.1 Ω loss, narrow band
Recommendation depends on space and ground plane
answer: Wavelength: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(433 × 10⁶) = 0.693 m.

answer.text: Sizes and electrical data:

head: Antenna
Size at 433 MHz
Input resistance
Directivity
Pattern
rows: λ/4 = 0.173 m over a ground plane
doughnut in the loop plane, null on the axis

answer: Efficiency: the dipole and monopole have R<sub>r</sub> tens of ohms against a loss of a fraction of an ohm, so η<sub>rad</sub> is above 95 %. The small loop has R<sub>r</sub> = 0.0197 Ω; with a realistic 0.1 Ω of copper and capacitor loss, η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.0197/0.1197 = 0.16, so its gain is 0.16 × 1.5 = 0.25, that is −6.0 dBi: about 8 dB below the dipole.

Matching and feed: the dipole is balanced and wants a balun on a coaxial feed; its 73 Ω suits 75 Ω, or 50 Ω with a VSWR of 1.46. The monopole is unbalanced and fits 50 Ω coax or a printed 50 Ω line directly, but it needs a ground plane of about λ/4 radius (17 cm) to give its ideal values; on a small board the board itself is the ground and the impedance and pattern change. The small loop is a tiny resistance in series with a large inductance; it must be tuned with a capacitor, and its high Q gives a narrow bandwidth that drifts with temperature and nearby objects.
Pattern: all three have a broad doughnut with D between 1.5 and 3.3, so none needs aiming. The loop’s null is on its axis; the dipole’s and the monopole’s are along the wire.

Evaluation: if a 17 cm whip and a metal case or board of similar size are acceptable, the monopole is the simplest and most efficient choice, fed directly from the radio’s 50 Ω output. If the sensor hangs free with no ground, a 33 cm dipole with a balun works best. The small loop fits inside a tiny case and is insensitive to a nearby hand (magnetic coupling), but it costs about 8 dB, which cuts the free-space range to about 40 per cent.

Bandwidth: the dipole and monopole have a usable bandwidth of a few per cent of 433 MHz, enough for the narrow ISM band. The small loop’s Q is set by its large reactance over its tiny resistance; for a 2.2 cm loop of 1 mm wire the inductance is about 44 nH, a reactance of about 120 Ω at 433 MHz, so Q ≈ 120/0.12 ≈ 1000 and the bandwidth is only about 0.4 MHz: it must be tuned in production and detunes easily.

answer.text: Decision table:

answer: Ground plane for the monopole: a printed monopole on a sensor board 5 cm across has a ground only about λ/14; the structure then behaves more like an off-centre dipole, its resistance moves away from 36.5 Ω and its gain falls towards the dipole value. The 5.16 dBi of the table needs a large plane and is an upper limit.

Link effect of the choice: with the same radio and the same receiving station, changing from the loop (−6 dBi) to the monopole (say 2 dBi on a real board) adds 8 dB, which multiplies the free-space range by 10<sup>8/20</sup> = 2.5.
Check: range scales as √(G<sub>t</sub>G<sub>r</sub>) at fixed power and sensitivity, so a gain loss of 8.2 dB (2.15 − (−6.0)) at one end cuts the free-space range by 10<sup>8.2/20</sup> = 2.6 times.

bank.q: Derive the fields of a Hertzian dipole from the retarded vector potential, identify the 1/r, 1/r² and 1/r³ terms, and hence find its radiated power, radiation resistance and directivity.
outline: Near terms store energy; far field E<sub>θ</sub> = jηβI₀l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr)
answer: Set-up: a straight element of length l ≪ λ along the z-axis at the origin, carrying a uniform phasor current I₀ (peak). Observation point at (r, θ, φ). Free space: μ₀, ε₀, η = √(μ₀/ε₀) = 120π Ω, β = ω√(μ₀ε₀) = 2π/λ.

answer.text: Vector potential. Since l ≪ r, every part of the element is at distance R ≈ r:
answer.pre:
A = (μ₀/4π) ∫ I e<sup>−jβR</sup>/R dl  →  A<sub>z</sub> = μ₀ I₀ l e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr)
A<sub>r</sub> = A<sub>z</sub> cos θ,   A<sub>θ</sub> = −A<sub>z</sub> sin θ,   A<sub>φ</sub> = 0

answer.text: Magnetic field. Only the φ component of the curl survives:
answer.pre:
H<sub>φ</sub> = (1/μ₀r)[∂(rA<sub>θ</sub>)/∂r − ∂A<sub>r</sub>/∂θ]
    = j β I₀ l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr) × [1 + 1/(jβr)]
H<sub>r</sub> = H<sub>θ</sub> = 0

answer.text: Electric field from Maxwell’s equation E = ∇ × H/(jωε₀):
answer.pre:
E<sub>r</sub> = η I₀ l cos θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(2πr²) × [1 + 1/(jβr)]
E<sub>θ</sub> = j η β I₀ l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr) × [1 + 1/(jβr) − 1/(βr)²]
E<sub>φ</sub> = 0

answer: The terms: in E<sub>θ</sub> the 1/r³ term (with 1/(βr)²) is the field of a static electric dipole of moment q l, the 1/r² term is the induction field (Biot–Savart for H<sub>φ</sub>), and the 1/r term is the radiation field. The near terms are 90° out of phase with the matching magnetic terms, so they hold stored energy that flows back each cycle; only the 1/r terms of E<sub>θ</sub> and H<sub>φ</sub> are in phase and carry net power. All terms are equal in size at βr = 1, r = λ/2π. E<sub>r</sub> has no 1/r term, so it vanishes far away.

answer.text: Far field (βr ≫ 1):
answer.pre:
E<sub>θ</sub> = j η β I₀ l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr),   H<sub>φ</sub> = E<sub>θ</sub>/η
|E<sub>θ</sub>| = 60π I₀ l sin θ/(λr)

answer.text: Radiated power. Power density S = |E<sub>θ</sub>|²/(2η); integrate over a sphere:
answer.pre:
P<sub>rad</sub> = ∫∫ S r² sin θ dθ dφ = (η β² I₀² l²/32π²) × 2π × (4/3)
      = η π (I₀ l/λ)²/3 = 40π² (I₀ l/λ)²   (η = 120π)

answer: Radiation resistance: ½ I₀² R<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>rad</sub> gives R<sub>r</sub> = 80π²(l/λ)² Ω. Directivity: U = r²S ∝ sin²θ, U<sub>max</sub> at θ = 90°, so D = 4πU<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>rad</sub> = 4π/(8π/3) = 1.5 (1.76 dBi). HPBW = 90°.

Wave impedance of the near field: dividing E<sub>θ</sub> by H<sub>φ</sub> gives Z = η[1 + 1/(jβr) − 1/(βr)²]/[1 + 1/(jβr)]. Its magnitude is about 3730 Ω at βr = 0.1, 267 Ω at βr = 1 and 373 Ω at βr = 10, approaching η = 377 Ω only far away: close to an electric dipole the field is mostly electric.

Power in the near terms: the complex Poynting vector ½ E × H* of the near terms is imaginary, so their time-average power is zero; it is reactive power that sets the large capacitive reactance of a short dipole. The real part of the power comes entirely from the 1/r terms, which is why the integral over a sphere of any radius gives the same P<sub>rad</sub>.
Half-power beamwidth check: sin²θ = 0.5 at 45° and 135°, so HPBW = 90°, and the doughnut is uniform in φ.

answer.text: The curl worked out for H<sub>φ</sub>:
answer.pre:
rA<sub>θ</sub> = −μ₀I₀l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4π)    →  ∂(rA<sub>θ</sub>)/∂r = jβ μ₀I₀l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4π)
∂A<sub>r</sub>/∂θ = −μ₀I₀l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr)
H<sub>φ</sub> = (1/μ₀r)[jβ μ₀I₀l sin θ/(4π) + μ₀I₀l sin θ/(4πr)] e<sup>−jβr</sup>
    = jβI₀l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr) × [1 + 1/(jβr)]

answer: Duality: a small loop of moment m = NIA gives the same fields with E and H exchanged (E<sub>φ</sub>, H<sub>r</sub>, H<sub>θ</sub>); its far field is E<sub>φ</sub> = 120π²NIA sin θ/(λ²r), so the derivation above also yields the loop by replacing I₀l with jβNIA.

Check with numbers: l = 1 cm, I₀ = 1 A, f = 1 GHz (λ = 0.3 m): R<sub>r</sub> = 0.877 Ω, P<sub>rad</sub> = 0.439 W; at 100 m broadside |E<sub>θ</sub>| = 60π × 0.01/(0.3 × 100) = 62.8 mV/m, and S = (0.0628)²/754 = 5.24 µW/m² equals 1.5 × 0.439/(4π × 10⁴) = 5.24 µW/m²: the field, the power and the directivity are consistent.

bank.q: A 2.4 GHz receiver needs −95 dBm. The transmitter gives 20 dBm, each antenna has 3 dBi gain and each side has 4 dB of cable and connector loss. Find the maximum free-space range, the range if a 10 dB fade margin is kept, and evaluate two ways to double the range.
outline: Allowed FSPL = EIRP + G<sub>r</sub> − L<sub>r</sub> − P<sub>sens</sub> = 113 dB
Solve 32.44 + 20 log f + 20 log d = 113: d = 4.44 km
With 10 dB margin: 103 dB, d = 1.41 km
Doubling range needs 6 dB: better antennas or less cable loss; EIRP limits
answer: Data: P<sub>t</sub> = 20 dBm, G<sub>t</sub> = G<sub>r</sub> = 3 dBi, L<sub>t</sub> = L<sub>r</sub> = 4 dB, P<sub>sens</sub> = −95 dBm, f = 2400 MHz, λ = 0.125 m.

answer.text: Budget for the largest path loss:

head: Item
Value
rows: Level that must reach the receiver

answer.text: Range with zero margin:
Range keeping a 10 dB fade margin:
answer.pre:
allowed FSPL = 113 − 10 = 103 dB
20 log₁₀ d<sub>km</sub> = 103 − 100.04 = 2.96  →  d = 1.41 km

answer: Range is 10<sup>10/20</sup> = 3.16 times shorter: every 20 dB of path loss is a factor of 10 in distance, every 6 dB a factor of 2.

To double the range (1.41 → 2.81 km) the budget needs 6.02 dB more. Option 1, better antennas: raising both antennas from 3 to 6 dBi adds 6 dB. This is cheap and also rejects interference from other directions, but higher gain means narrower beams that must be aimed, and the EIRP rises from 19 to 22 dBm, which must stay within the band’s regulatory EIRP limit. Option 2, less cable loss: moving the radios to the antennas (or using low-loss cable) cuts 4 + 4 dB to, say, 1 + 1 dB, gaining 6 dB with no change in EIRP beyond 3 dB and no aiming. Raising the transmit power by 6 dB works only in one direction of a two-way link and also raises EIRP.

At the 1.41 km point the received power is exactly the −85 dBm that leaves 10 dB above sensitivity. The power density there is S = EIRP/(4πd²) = 0.0794 W/(4π × 1405²) = 3.20 × 10⁻⁹ W/m², a field of only 1.55 mV/m.

The same hardware at 5 GHz instead of 2.4 GHz: FSPL rises by 20 log₁₀(5/2.4) = 6.38 dB at every distance, so with the same antenna gains the range falls by the factor 5/2.4 = 2.08: 4.44 km becomes 2.13 km, and 1.41 km becomes 0.67 km. Keeping the same antenna size instead of the same gain would recover this, because the gain of a fixed aperture rises as f².

Range scales as 10<sup>ΔdB/20</sup>: +6 dB doubles it, +20 dB multiplies it by 10. That is why decibels are the natural language of link planning: every improvement, in antenna, cable, power or receiver, is added on the same scale.

Each answer above is the free-space ceiling. A real 2.4 GHz link through trees or buildings loses 10 to 30 dB more, so planners take measured path-loss models and keep the 10 dB margin on top of them, not instead of them.

answer.text: Range against kept margin (same budget, 113 dB allowed):

answer: A third lever is the receiver: lowering the data rate narrows the bandwidth and improves sensitivity (each halving of bandwidth gives about 3 dB), which also extends range without raising EIRP.

Evaluation: cutting the feeder loss is the most efficient fix here, because 8 dB of cable loss is wasted on both ends; it helps both directions of the link and adds no interference. Friis assumes free space; at ground level at 2.4 GHz, walls, trees and ground reflections will cost more than the 10 dB kept, so the real outdoor range will be shorter.

bank.q: State and explain the reciprocity theorem for antennas, and show that the maximum effective aperture of any antenna is Dλ²/4π, working it out for the Hertzian dipole. Use them to justify measuring an antenna’s gain on transmit and using it on receive.
outline: Z₁₂ = Z₂₁ for two antennas in a linear, isotropic medium
Consequences: same pattern, impedance, gain in both roles
Hertzian dipole: P<sub>L</sub> = E²λ²/(640π²), S = E²/(240π), A<sub>em</sub> = 3λ²/8π = 1.5λ²/4π
A<sub>em</sub>/D = λ²/4π for all antennas; half-wave dipole 0.13λ²
Range measurement; half-wave dipole numbers at 100 MHz
answer: Reciprocity theorem: if a current I₁ at the terminals of antenna 1 produces an open-circuit voltage V₂ at antenna 2, then the same current at antenna 2 produces the same open-circuit voltage at antenna 1. In network terms the two antennas form a two-port with Z₁₂ = Z₂₁. It holds in any linear, passive, isotropic medium (air, ordinary dielectrics and metals), whatever the two antennas are.

Consequences: (1) the receiving pattern of an antenna equals its transmitting pattern, because moving antenna 2 round antenna 1 maps the same transfer impedance either way; (2) the self-impedance Z₁₁ is the same in both roles, so a match made on transmit holds on receive; (3) the gain on transmit and the effective aperture on receive are tied by one universal constant, shown below.

answer.text: Effective aperture of the Hertzian dipole (uniform current, l ≪ λ), wave arriving broadside and matched:
answer.pre:
V<sub>oc</sub> = E l                         (l<sub>eff</sub> = l)
P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>oc</sub>²/(8R<sub>r</sub>) = E² l²/(8 × 80π² l²/λ²) = E² λ²/(640π²)
S = E²/(2η) = E²/(240π)
A<sub>em</sub> = P<sub>L</sub>/S = 240π λ²/(640π²) = 3λ²/(8π) = 1.5 × λ²/(4π)

answer: Since D = 1.5 for this dipole, A<sub>em</sub> = Dλ²/4π. By reciprocity, if two antennas face each other, the power transfer is the same in both directions for identical set-ups, which forces A<sub>em</sub>/D to be the same for both antennas. The dipole fixes the constant, so A<sub>em</sub>/D = λ²/4π for every antenna, and with loss A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/4π. For a half-wave dipole A<sub>em</sub> = 1.64λ²/4π = 0.13λ²; for an isotropic antenna λ²/4π = 0.0796λ².

Justification of the measurement practice: an antenna range drives the antenna under test as a transmitter and measures its pattern and gain (for example by comparison with a standard horn). Reciprocity guarantees that the same pattern applies on receive, and A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/4π converts the measured gain into the receiving aperture. The same reasoning lets one dish serve both directions of a satellite or radar link.

answer.text: Numerical check, half-wave dipole at 100 MHz (λ = 3 m) in a 1 mV/m field:

answer: Equivalent circuit on receive: the antenna is a source V<sub>oc</sub> in series with Z<sub>A</sub>. With a conjugate-matched load the load takes |V<sub>oc</sub>|²/8R<sub>A</sub>, and for a lossless antenna the same power is re-radiated through R<sub>r</sub>; A<sub>em</sub> is defined with this matched load.

answer.text: Using reciprocity in a gain measurement (two identical antennas): measure P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>t</sub> at a known distance and solve Friis for G. Two identical horns at 10 GHz (λ = 0.03 m), 3 m apart:
answer.pre:
measured P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>t</sub> = 6.33 × 10⁻³  (−22.0 dB)
G = (4πd/λ) √(P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>t</sub>) = (4π × 3/0.03) × 0.0796 = 100  (20 dBi)

answer: The method works only because the two antennas have the same gain in both roles; the horns are about 12 cm across, so 2D²/λ ≈ 1 m and 3 m is in the far field.

Why the constant is universal: place antenna 1 (gain D₁, area A₁) and antenna 2 (D₂, A₂) facing each other. Power sent from 1 to 2 is P D₁ A₂/(4πd²); from 2 to 1 it is P D₂ A₁/(4πd²). Reciprocity makes them equal for identical set-ups, so A₁/D₁ = A₂/D₂: the ratio of aperture to directivity is the same for every antenna.

In general the receiving area includes every loss: A<sub>e</sub> = η<sub>rad</sub>(1 − |Γ|²) × PLF × Dλ²/4π. The ideal A<sub>em</sub> = Dλ²/4π assumes a lossless antenna, a conjugate-matched load and a polarization-matched wave.

Limits: reciprocity fails in non-reciprocal media (magnetized ferrite, the ionosphere in the Earth’s field), and equal received powers need equal source and load conditions; the transfer impedances are always equal, the powers only when the set-ups match.

bank.q: Explain the reactive near-field, radiating near-field and far-field regions with a labelled sketch, derive the 2D²/λ boundary, and describe what goes wrong if a pattern is measured too close. Illustrate with a 0.6 m dish at 12 GHz.
outline: Field terms 1/r³, 1/r², 1/r; stored versus radiated energy
Too-close measurement: broadened beam, filled nulls, low gain; DTH dish 1.82 m and 28.8 m
answer: Around any antenna the field contains terms falling as 1/r³ and 1/r² (stored, reactive energy that flows out and back each cycle) and a term falling as 1/r (radiation). Their balance divides space into three regions.

answer.text: Sketch (antenna at the left, distance increasing to the right):

svg.aria: An antenna at the left and three bands to its right: reactive near field up to 0.62 root D cubed over lambda, radiating near field up to 2 D squared over lambda, then far field.

answer: Reactive near field, r < 0.62√(D³/λ): stored energy dominates, E and H are not in phase, and the wave impedance is far from 377 Ω (thousands of ohms close to a short dipole). Radiating near field (Fresnel), up to 2D²/λ: radiation dominates but the angular shape of the field still depends on r. Far field (Fraunhofer), r > 2D²/λ with r ≫ D and r ≫ λ: the pattern no longer changes with distance, E ⊥ H ⊥ r, E/H = 377 Ω and S ∝ 1/r².

answer.text: Derivation of 2D²/λ. For a point on the axis at distance r from an aperture of size D, the extra path from the rim is
answer.pre:
Δ = √(r² + (D/2)²) − r ≈ D²/(8r)        (r ≫ D)
phase error = 2πΔ/λ ≤ π/8   →   D²/(8r) ≤ λ/16   →   r ≥ 2D²/λ

answer: For an electrically small antenna 2D²/λ is shorter than a wavelength and meaningless; then the wavelength rules: the reactive zone ends near λ/2π and the induction term falls to a tenth of the radiation term by about 1.6λ.

answer.text: Worked illustration, DTH dish D = 0.6 m at 12 GHz (λ = 0.025 m):

answer: Measuring too close: at 20 m from that dish the rim-to-centre path difference is 0.36/160 = 2.25 mm = 0.09λ, a phase error of 32° instead of at most 22.5°. The partial cancellation broadens the measured main beam and lowers its peak, fills in the nulls, and raises and smears the side lobes, so the gain is underestimated and the side-lobe level looks worse than it is. Inside the reactive region the probe also couples to the stored field and loads the antenna, changing its input impedance.
Wave impedance as a marker of the regions (Hertzian dipole): |E<sub>θ</sub>/H<sub>φ</sub>| ≈ 3730 Ω at βr = 0.1, 267 Ω at βr = 1 and 373 Ω at βr = 10, settling to 377 Ω only well into the far field.

Remedies when the far-field distance is too long to build: a compact range, where a large reflector turns the spherical wave of a feed into a plane wave over a few metres, or a near-field scanner, which measures amplitude and phase on a surface in the radiating near field and computes the far-field pattern by a Fourier transform. Both are standard for dishes and arrays whose 2D²/λ runs to hundreds of metres.

Pattern in the Fresnel region of a uniformly lit aperture: the phase error grows towards the rim, so the edge contributions add slightly out of step. The main beam “defocuses”: for a uniformly lit circular aperture the on-axis gain falls by about 0.06 dB at 2D²/λ and about 0.9 dB at a quarter of that distance, and the first nulls fill in.

Small antennas follow the wavelength instead. For a 15 cm whip at 100 MHz (λ = 3 m), 2D²/λ = 0.015 m is meaningless; the reactive zone extends to about λ/2π = 0.48 m and the far field starts at about 1.6λ = 4.8 m. A phone at the ear is inside the reactive zone of its antenna, which is why its exposure is assessed by measured SAR, not from far-field gain.
Check: at exactly 28.8 m the path difference is 0.36/230.4 = 1.5625 mm = λ/16, the π/8 limit.

glossary.def: A structure that turns a guided wave on a line into a free-space wave, or the reverse.
An imaginary antenna radiating equally in all directions; directivity 1 (0 dBi).
A potential built from each source current as it was R/c seconds earlier; in phasor form, the factor e<sup>−jβR</sup>.
A current element much shorter than a wavelength with the same current along its length.
Power radiated per unit solid angle, U = r²S, in W/sr.
Average power crossing unit area, S = |E|²/(2η) in the far field, in W/m².
The lobe of a pattern that contains the direction of maximum radiation.
Any lobe other than the main lobe; side lobes lie beside it and the back lobe opposite it.
The main-lobe peak divided by the radiation in the opposite direction, usually in dB.
Ω<sub>A</sub> = ∯ P<sub>n</sub> dΩ, the solid angle the power would fill at peak intensity; D = 4π/Ω<sub>A</sub>.
Gain in decibels relative to an isotropic radiator and to a half-wave dipole; dBd = dBi − 2.15.
η<sub>rad</sub> = R<sub>r</sub>/(R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>), the share of the accepted power that is radiated.
The series resistance R<sub>L</sub> that accounts for heat in the conductors, dielectric and coils of an antenna.
The effective area of a horn or dish divided by its physical area, typically 0.5 to 0.7 for a dish.
−20 log₁₀|Γ| in dB: how far the reflected power is below the incident power at the antenna terminals; larger is better.
(1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), the voltage standing wave ratio on the feed line; 1 for a perfect match.
Major over minor axis of the polarization ellipse: 1 for circular, infinite for linear.
The fraction of power a receiving antenna takes from a wave of another polarization, |ρ̂<sub>w</sub> · ρ̂<sub>a</sub>|².
The region within about 0.62√(D³/λ) of a large antenna (λ/2π of a small one) where stored energy dominates.
The radiating near field, between the reactive region and 2D²/λ, where the pattern still changes with distance.
The far field, beyond 2D²/λ, where the pattern is fixed and the wave is locally plane.
A device that joins a balanced antenna such as a dipole to an unbalanced line such as coaxial cable.
Replacing a perfect ground plane by a mirror image of the source, used to analyse the monopole.
m = NIA for an N-turn loop of area A carrying current I, directed along the loop axis.
The length l<sub>eff</sub> for which V<sub>oc</sub> = E l<sub>eff</sub>; λ/π for a half-wave dipole.
Effective isotropic radiated power, P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub> (less feeder loss), the transmitter’s strength in its best direction.
(4πd/λ)², the spreading term of the Friis equation; 32.44 + 20 log₁₀ f<sub>MHz</sub> + 20 log₁₀ d<sub>km</sub> in dB.
The weakest signal, in dBm, at which a receiver still meets its specified error rate.
The decibels a link budget keeps above the sensitivity to survive fading, rain and misalignment.
